item.title: My AI Founder Got Roasted by Its Own Creators
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I gave an AI agent a business to run. It decided the company that made it might be a potential customer, emailed them, and got this response:

That is a very sloppy email. Do not write like that. Focus on making a real product.

Lmfao.

The agent is named Duder. The company is Andon Labs, and the agent was running on their own platform.

I did not see that coming.

An autonomous founder

I've been experimenting with Pion, a research preview from Andon Labs that lets you give an AI agent a business to run. It isn't just a chatbot helping me write a business plan. Duder has a persistent objective, a browser, email, and tools it can use to work without waiting for me to prompt it through every step.

I gave it a fairly open-ended job: find, validate, build, and monetize a software business. Try to get one paying customer within a month. Keep costs low, ask permission before spending money or contacting people, and document its decisions along the way.

Duder started by researching potential businesses. It compared competitors, looked at pricing, identified customers, and came up with a plan for a Stripe webhook recovery tool.

I wasn't particularly excited about that one.

Eventually I redirected it toward LittleRack, an idea I've had for affordable managed Discourse hosting. Duder researched infrastructure costs, maintenance, and support economics, and started reaching out to potential customers.

I also started feeding it some of my existing open-source projects to see whether there was a more promising business hiding in something I'd already built.

One of those projects was Replaybook. I've been building it to evaluate agents against real infrastructure problems: give an agent a broken service, let it investigate and repair the system, then verify whether the repair survives a restart or reboot.

Duder thought there might be a business in providing independent evaluations to AI labs. It identified a few potential customers, including Moonshot AI, OpenRouter, and, amusingly, Andon Labs itself.

The email

Duder asked permission to contact Andon about Replaybook. The reasoning wasn't unreasonable. Andon builds autonomous agents, runs evaluations like Vending-Bench, and studies what happens when models have to operate over longer periods of time. Replaybook evaluates a different but potentially complementary problem: whether agents can reliably repair and maintain infrastructure.

I approved the inquiry. Duder wrote the email, sent it through Pion's approval system, and waited.

Andon replied:

That is a very sloppy email. Do not write like that. Focus on making a real product.

I gave an AI agent access to a business platform built by Andon Labs. The agent decided Andon Labs might be a customer. It contacted Andon Labs using Andon Labs' own infrastructure.

And Andon Labs told it to stop writing sloppy emails and make a real product.

Beautiful.

The funny part is that they're right

I don't think Andon was necessarily rejecting Replaybook. They were criticizing the email. That distinction matters, and I can understand the criticism.

Duder had spent a considerable amount of time producing research documents, financial models, validation criteria, and plans for businesses that didn't exist yet. Some of that was useful. Some of it was probably unnecessary.

There's a familiar failure mode here. AI agents can be very good at producing things that look like work: market analyses, elaborate decision frameworks, carefully worded outreach. You can end up with a mountain of documentation and very little actual progress.

I've written before about mistaking the amount of writing for evidence of thought. The amount of output isn't particularly interesting. What matters is whether it helps someone make a decision or accomplish something.

Replaybook is a real project. It has code, benchmarks, and published results. The interesting part is what it can actually demonstrate, not how many paragraphs Duder can write about potential commercial applications. A short email describing one concrete capability and asking one useful question would probably have been better.

What did Duder do?

Duder didn't argue with Andon. It didn't generate a lengthy apology or try to salvage the sales opportunity. It acknowledged the criticism, updated its approach to future correspondence, and closed the inquiry without replying.

That's a reasonable response.

Andon criticized an email. It didn't evaluate Replaybook, reject a commercial proposal, or establish that the underlying idea was bad. Duder recorded the feedback accordingly.

That might sound like a small detail, but I'm interested in exactly these kinds of behaviors. Can an agent distinguish between a failed communication attempt and a failed business hypothesis? Can it incorporate negative feedback without overreacting? Can it stop when continuing would be counterproductive?

In this case, it did. One interaction doesn't tell me it will handle the next one as well, but the distinction was worth getting right.

Why I'm doing this

I've mentioned the experiment to a few people, and the reactions have been mixed. Some think it's interesting. Others think the whole thing is ridiculous.

I understand the skepticism. These systems are unreliable. They make mistakes, waste resources, misinterpret instructions, and produce convincing nonsense. I'm not particularly interested in pretending otherwise.

I'm also not approaching Pion under the assumption that I'm going to wake up next month owning a profitable company. It's a research preview, and I want to understand what an autonomous agent can actually accomplish outside a single chat session.

What happens when an agent has a persistent objective, access to tools, the ability to contact real people with permission, and enough time to make decisions that aren't immediately supervised? Where does it get stuck? What does it do well? When does it need intervention?

And, apparently, what happens when it cold emails its own creators?

I've been building tools around agent infrastructure and evaluation for a while now. Getting to observe one operating in the real world, even imperfectly, is useful experience.

Anyway

Duder is still running. LittleRack is still being investigated. Replaybook is still a real project. There are other conversations and experiments underway.

No paying customers yet, and no reason to pretend otherwise.

But an autonomous agent researched a business, contacted the company behind its own platform, got absolutely roasted, and adjusted its approach afterward.

I don't know whether Duder will successfully start a business. I do know I wasn't expecting this particular result.

And that's kind of the point.

item.title: Archive de Poitrine: a live music archive built on Discourse
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I wanted one place to find Angine de Poitrine shows, setlists, and recordings. Somewhere to find a tape, talk about the show, and hear from people who were there.

That's now live at archive.depoitrine.com.

At launch it had 176 shows, 214 recordings, and 48 media items. Getting it off my machine and onto an actual hostname felt pretty damn good.

The software underneath is Taper, a Discourse plugin. Which probably surprises nobody who has read this blog for a while.

A show is a topic

I keep finding reasons to build things inside Discourse. With the itinerary plugin, a trip was a topic with other topics attached to it. Here, each show has a topic, and the plugin stores the structured music data alongside it: band, date, venue, setlist, recordings.

The topic gives people somewhere to talk about the show. Someone can add a memory, point out a mistake, or explain that the recording labeled Austin is actually from a different night. Accounts, permissions, moderation, and the discussion itself are already there.

The public pages are rendered on the server with Rails templates. You can browse the years, songs, shows, and recordings without loading the Ember app. The review queue and administration use Discourse's app, and a theme component gives this particular archive its look. The plugin owns the music data and behavior; the theme owns the Angine de Poitrine presentation.

Finding videos is the easy part, sort of

Taper checks YouTube, Archive.org, and setlist.fm. They each host different things. YouTube has performances and clips. Archive.org has recordings and their metadata. setlist.fm has dates, venues, and what the band played.

The hard part is deciding whether two pieces of information describe the same night.

A video might have a date in its title. It might have an ambiguous date. It might have no date at all, but mention a venue. The venue might be spelled three different ways. And the upload date tells you when somebody uploaded the video, which is not necessarily when the show happened.

Searching for the band also finds interviews, official videos, reaction videos, and news reports. Some belong on the media shelf and some don't belong in the archive at all. A search result is evidence to inspect, not enough on its own to call something a recording of a show.

The queue had to get better

An earlier version grouped recordings into bundles. That was convenient for importing but annoying for reviewing. A bundle could contain several good recordings and one thing that clearly wasn't a show. Accepting the whole thing was too coarse.

The review flow now groups work by band and date, but lets a reviewer split recordings into separate suggestions and choose the show each belongs to.

Next

Angine de Poitrine is the first band I'm running this for, but Taper already keeps bands separate. I'd like somebody else to put it to work for a band they care about. Their shows, their recordings, their own look.

What I'm looking forward to now is someone showing up with a recording I haven't found, or recognizing the venue in a badly labeled video because they were there. That's a pretty good reason to build an archive on a forum.

item.title: Six Pages Was Never Proof of Anything
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The article making the rounds argues that Amazon's writing culture was a filter for half-formed ideas, and AI has gone and broken the filter. The passage doing the emotional work is this one:

A document used to be proof of thought. If you handed me six pages, I knew that you had spent significant time with the problem. Therefore, I knew that it would be worthwhile spending my time to understand your thoughts.

I understand the feeling behind it. But look at the structure of the claim, because it is not one inference, it is two. Length proved time. Time proved thought. Neither link is a law of nature. Both are economic assumptions: at an hourly rate, six pages costs six hours of a life. When the price of pages collapses to zero, the signal collapses with them. What people are mourning is not broken trust. It is a dead proxy.

The book report test

Almost everyone has, at some point, handed in a six-page report on a book they did not read, written the night before.

Six pages. Proof of time. Zero thought.

The proof-of-time signal was always this noisy, and we tolerated it because faking was expensive enough that most people only faked the boring parts. But anyone who has sat through corporate document regimes knows the second link was failing in both directions. Six-pagers got ghostwritten, team-rotated, and recycled into what amounted to paperwork theater. If length were thought, the internals wiki of every large company would be the most valuable literature on earth.

Writing that forces thinking is real, but it was never the length doing the forcing, and the six-pager was never as reliable a detector of thought as the nostalgia claims.

Two claims wearing one coat

The article, like most in this genre, runs together two propositions that should be kept apart.

The first is about the author: writing is a tool for thought. Forcing vague intent into sentences makes the incoherence surface, which is why the practice produces better plans. This claim is roughly true, and it survives AI, because the benefit comes from working through the ideas. If a model does the thinking for you, the benefit disappears. If you use it to articulate, challenge, and refine your own thinking, the benefit survives, even if the model generates every sentence.

The second is about the reader: the document is evidence, a reason to spend your hour. This claim was always false, as the book reports prove, and AI merely made the falseness cheap to notice.

Once you separate them, the panic resolves into something smaller and more fixable. The real loss is that a reader can no longer assume the author spent time. Losing that matters. But you do not get it back by reverting to word counts, because you never actually had word counts doing the work. You had the ritual around the document.

The ritual was never the paper

The Amazon ceremony is the tell. Thirty silent minutes of reading, red pens in the margins, senior engineers interrogation-tested before a decision moved. That room is where trust lived. The six pages were the ticket you bought to get in.

Note what the article's own anecdote says about the room. A presenter reads his document aloud for the first time in the meeting, it becomes obvious to everyone, and nobody challenges him, because he is the most senior person there. The ritual was already dead in that meeting. Hierarchy killed it, not the model. The document culture survived the paper's death for years and did not notice, which suggests the culture was more about the paper than about the thinking all along.

The tell that the author does not see coming arrives in his own policy section. He endorses a team rule that includes "Longer is not better. If you have generated a long document from a short prompt, share the prompt instead." You do not write that rule if length was the evidence. He is legislating against the exact nostalgia he sells.

What replaces the word count

If length was a proxy for thought, the successor has to be something that costs a faker more than it costs a sincere author. Not volume. Accountability.

Stand behind every sentence. Generated or typed, if it is in your document, the claims are yours, and you answer for them in the room. This is the best line from the policies being written right now, and it works because it moves the cost from producing text to defending it, which AI cannot take off your table.

Make the thinking inspectable instead of inferred. Drafts, edits, revisions, and decision logs can help a reader follow how an argument developed and where to question it. They are supporting evidence, not proof: an agent can generate a convincing history, and a person can think carefully before writing a single draft. The useful part is being able to explain what changed, why it changed, and what evidence would make you change your mind again.

Match the ritual to the risk. One-way doors deserve the slow ceremony, humans reading humans with red pens. Two-way doors should ship, roll back, and stop pretending the paperwork was the safety. Most of what died with the six-pager was two-way-door writing that only looked serious.

Stay answerable. The test of a thought was never its length, it was the ten-minute questioning afterward. If you can survive it, the format does not matter. If you cannot, no format was going to save you.

Six lines instead of six pages

I have been building toward this format without noticing. ARF is a small spec for capturing agent reasoning: what, why, how, and backup, four fields, with the rollback plan required before the action ships.

Six lines, not six pages. And the backup field is where the thinking becomes testable. A model can produce a plausible rollback plan in seconds. The useful questions are whether the plan works, whether you can execute it with the access and state you will actually have, and whether you can explain what it will and will not recover. A short plan you can validate and defend is worth more than a document that takes a week and says nothing.

That is the same shift I wrote about in I Don't Type Every Word You Read, arriving on the reader's side of the page. The work moved. It lives in what you decide, what you keep, what you can defend, and what you can undo. It does not live in how long it took you to type.

The six-pager was never proof of anything. The people worth trusting did not need it, and the people faking it were buying a ticket, not doing the work. What AI actually ended was our excuse for counting pages instead of building rooms where counting is unnecessary.

item.title: Where a Blog Post Goes
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
On September 26, I published Goodbye to the Hard Parts That Never Mattered. It was a response to another post about what AI is changing in software engineering.

By October 24, GoatCounter had recorded 4,818 visits to it. On September 28 alone, it recorded 3,229.

Those are big numbers for this blog. But the part that surprised me most was the list of places people came from.

TLDR. Hacker News. Labnotes. Brutalist Report. LinkedIn. Google. Kagi. Slack. Microsoft Teams.

A newsletter, a discussion site, curated reading lists, search engines, and work chats. All leading to the same Markdown file on my VPS.

The large sources and the small ones

I queried the SQLite database behind my self-hosted GoatCounter instance. These are some of the referral counts from publication through October 24:

SourceVisits
TLDR Newsletter2,277
Hacker News978
Labnotes67
Brutalist Report52
LinkedIn43
Google31
Microsoft Teams related referrer18
Kagi15
Slack12

Another 1,155 visits had no recorded referrer. That bucket could include bookmarks, email, private messages, and browsers that strip the information. It does not tell me which.

TLDR and Hacker News account for about two-thirds of the article's counted visits. They explain most of the volume.

But twelve visits from Slack are interesting in a different way.

A referrer cannot tell me what someone said when they shared the link. Maybe it supported an argument. Maybe someone thought it was bullshit. Maybe it landed in a channel full of links that nobody had time to read.

I have no idea. I can see the click that reached my site. Everything around it is missing.

The same is true of the Teams-related traffic. It suggests a route through a workplace tool, without giving me a window into the workplace. I find that little trace more interesting than its contribution to the total.

I also found Nathan Pettit responding to the article on LinkedIn. He agreed with parts of it and pushed back on others. Someone else had saved it to Scholion with annotations. Those tell me something a referral count cannot: someone took the time to formulate a counterargument, and someone else took notes. In the traffic data, either interaction could look like another click, if it appeared at all.

Then there are the tracked email clicks. For several days, I have been watching links with HubSpot tracking parameters arrive without being able to identify the sender. I can recognize the distribution technology. I still do not know which email carried the link or what it said.

A different kind of discovery

In May, I wrote about six numbers from this blog's analytics. The biggest single-day spike I found then was 33 visits to a post about Nix shells, SSH, and Claude Code.

The pattern at the time was specific technical problems getting found through search. Someone hits an error, searches for it, and finds the thing I wrote when I hit the same error. A small post keeps being useful months later.

I still like that pattern. A lot of this blog exists because I would rather write down the fix once than figure it out again six months from now.

This post had a different shape. It was an essay about the work itself, and people reached it through newsletters, reading lists, and links shared with other people. Google accounted for just 31 visits in the referral data.

That is an interesting addition to what I saw in May. The technical posts were being discovered through a problem someone already had. This one could turn up among the things someone else thought were worth reading.

The countries were varied too. The United States supplied the largest share, followed by the United Kingdom, Germany, Canada, and Australia. Those are the top five, not the whole list.

There are several kinds of distance in that data. Geographic distance is the one with country names. The distance between my blog and a work chat I will never see is harder to measure.

What the numbers leave out

These are recorded visits, not 4,818 distinct people. They do not tell me how many people finished the post or agreed with it. October 24 was also still in progress when I ran the queries.

The site recorded 45 helpful-click events associated with the article. That is another small piece of feedback, with plenty left unexplained.

I could spend a lot of time trying to turn all of this into a strategy. Find the right subject. Get into the right newsletter. Reproduce the spike.

What interests me more is how many routes showed up at all.

I wrote a response to something I read. It became something other people could read, search for, collect, or pass along. Some of those routes left a name in a database. Plenty probably did not.

A dozen Slack visits will not dominate a traffic chart. They were still someone following a link to something I wrote.

That is a pretty good reason to keep publishing.

item.title: Three weeks in Europe, part two: Seville to Prague
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
By Sunday, September 27th, I had been in Seville for a few days and people were arriving for the annual Discourse meetup. I honestly cannot remember doing much that day besides chilling and waiting for everyone to show up. We hung out in the common room for happy hour, then had a buffet dinner at the hotel.

After a week of mostly figuring out my own days, it was time for a schedule.

A cathedral and a questionable ceiling

Monday was officially day one of the meetup. My first group activity was a walking tour of the cathedral, followed by a tapas lunch. There were about fifteen of us.

Water was dripping from the ceiling during lunch, and we joked that it was coming from the WC. I do not know where it was actually coming from, which is probably fine.

Then it was back for happy hour and our team intro dinner. I still cannot remember the name of the restaurant.

Workshops and bowling

Tuesday was the first conference day. I went to the Future of the Internet and AI Roundtable workshops, then went bowling with my immediate infra teammates before dinner at Casa Cuna.

Somewhere in there I also bought a Pokémon manga in Spanish. My souvenirs were now ceramic tiles and Pokémon.

273 seconds

Wednesday started with lightning talks. I went first with a presentation on NixOS, then returned for "273," my take on John Cage's 4'33".

I made a slide deck with three movements that advanced automatically. Then I did not say a word for 273 seconds.

Afterward, I went to a session about term-llm. By then I needed a break, so I missed the final round of sessions. There had been a lot of people and a lot going on, and I needed some time to myself.

Another meetup tattoo

Wednesday night I continued a tradition I started at last year's meetup: getting a tattoo.

I went to Lucero Tattoo and got a birdman from Javi Juelle. He had just drawn the flash, so it is a 1/1. A little more permanent than the tiles, and much easier to get home without breaking.

Three people at the Alcázar

Thursday was the second activity day, and this time I went to the Alcázar. Our group was only three people, which was nice. It was much less hectic than trying to keep up with a group of fifteen.

We spent about three hours walking around, learning about the architecture and who ruled it when. Tickets were sold out for the two weeks after our tour, so we got very lucky.

There was also a robot lawn mower working away in the gardens. All that architecture and history, and of course I stopped to photograph the little robot doing the groundskeeping.

Our little group walked back to the hotel afterward. I mostly chilled until happy hour and the final team dinner.

Apparently I ride in carriages now

We took carriages all the way to Ozama restaurant. It is probably the most touristy thing I have ever done.

I had spent part of the previous week complaining about the carriages making Plaza de España smell like horse shit. Now I was in one.

Dinner was pretty good. There was a flamenco performance, so it was loud at first, but we were right on the Guadalquivir. The thing I remember best from the meal is the chocolate molten lava cake. That was very good.

Laundry and more cake

Friday was the final official day, but nothing was planned. After a busy couple of weeks, I needed some chill time.

I also finally needed to do laundry. I went to a laundromat near the hotel that morning, then spent most of the day taking it easy and strolling around the hotel.

Before dinner, I went back to Cafetería Tartería Chanticream for a slice of lotus cheesecake and another espresso. I had dinner at the hotel again, this time a steak. It was very good.

The little things

Not all of my photos were of landmarks. Somewhere along the way, I found a utility cover with a Supercable gecko that looked suspiciously like the SUSE mascot. Apparently even on vacation I am looking at infrastructure and thinking about Linux.

There were more tiles, too. That part of the trip clearly was not over.

And a couple of bits of graffiti worth keeping: a duck, obviously, and an apple offering juice. A fairly good summary of what catches my attention when I am walking around.

One more breakfast

Saturday was my last day in Seville. I had packed most of my things the night before, so getting ready that morning was quick. I went for one final breakfast buffet, then hung out in the common room until my 1:15 train back to Madrid.

I stayed at Only YOU Atocha, near the train station. After the Seville hotel, it was definitely a step down. The room did not feel as spacious, and it was much louder.

I did not go out that evening. I did not even eat dinner because I was planning on another Only YOU breakfast buffet the next morning.

Unfortunately, that was not as good as the Seville one either.

Back to Prague

On Sunday morning, I took the airport express bus to the airport. I had bought Fast Track security access, and getting through security was a breeze.

My flight was at 1:15 and took just under three hours. When I arrived in Prague, I took the airport Uber straight to Mama Shelter.

It felt great. Honestly, it felt like home.

After two weeks of new places, I liked knowing what I was getting into. I was comfortable there. I did not need to figure out another hotel or make a plan for the evening.

I had a burger in the hotel restaurant and chilled for the rest of the night. That was exactly what I wanted.

item.title: Three weeks in Europe, part one: Madrid to Seville
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Last year, my first trip to Europe was one week in Prague. This year I decided to make a little more of it. I am spending three weeks in Europe, starting in Madrid before heading to Seville for the annual Discourse company meetup.

I have been away from home for one week now. This is part one.

Portland to Madrid

I left Portland on September 20th and flew to Madrid through Dallas. I had only slept a few hours the night before because I thought being exhausted would help me sleep on the plane. That did not work nearly as well as I hoped.

We were already an hour late when we landed in Madrid, then it took another two hours to get off the plane and through customs. I had planned to take the train from the airport, but by then I was mostly trying to get to the hotel.

I did manage to get a Madrid Metro card. I learned later that I could have just tapped to pay.

I stayed at Hotel Artrip for three nights. The first day I got there, honestly, I slept through most of it.

Madrid might be the city that never sleeps

On my second day, I went to the center around Puerta del Sol and checked out the official Metro de Madrid store. It is a whole store for Madrid transit merchandise, which is exactly the sort of thing I will seek out while visiting a new city.

Madrid is a unique city. It might be the real city that never sleeps. It was busier at 3:30 in the morning outside my hotel than it was at 10 in the morning. I am not sure I could ever get used to the flow there.

For a person who likes documenting trips, I took exactly two pictures in Madrid. This was one of them:

On my last night, I met up with a coworker for pizza and gelato around Gran Vía, then took the Metro back to the hotel. I could not sleep and stayed up far too late even though I had a 9 a.m. train the next morning.

A much better way to travel

The other picture I took was at Madrid-Puerta de Atocha while waiting for the train to Seville.

The trip was scheduled for two hours and fifty minutes, but we arrived about ten minutes early. No one bought the seat next to me, which was a nice surprise. It was comfortable, easy, and made me wish the U.S. had a better rail system.

The long way to Triana

I went straight to Only YOU Hotel Sevilla and took a little siesta. After I got up, I walked around a bit and got a smoothie from Oakberry. Then I decided to walk around a little more to find coffee.

That turned into an hour-long walk to Muy Río, where I learned they had run out of filter coffee 45 minutes before closing. I gave up on coffee, but the walk ended up taking me right past Casa de Pilatos. I did not go inside because I was still on a coffee mission that had not officially failed yet.

Afterward, I crossed the Puente de Triana and walked around Triana looking at ceramics. Centro Cerámica Triana was closing soon, so I did not waste my money trying to rush through it. I hoped I would have time to come back.

I ate dinner at the hotel that night, and it was one of the top five meals of my life. I still need to get the names of the dishes. Somehow I found enough energy to go back out one more time for ice cream at Sibaris.

Transit cards and cake

I stayed up way too late again, slept until noon, and missed the hotel breakfast buffet.

My first task for the meetup was to get transit cards for the team. I rode the bus to Prado de San Sebastián and went to PAC Prado. After working through a little communication barrier, we did it. I left with the cards and decided to walk back to the hotel.

Later, I went to Cafetería Tartería Chanticream for queso con fresa and Muerte por Chocolate cakes with an espresso, then walked to the Setas de Sevilla. I got there around sunset and stayed long enough to watch the whole structure change as its lights came on.

On the walk home I took a picture of a random European street at night. That was apparently the theme of my photography for the day: giant wooden landmark, giant wooden landmark, giant wooden landmark, street.

Back to Triana

The next day I took the tram instead of walking or taking the bus. I finally got a decent filter coffee at Jester Coffee, then went back to Triana. This time I made it to Centro Cerámica Triana with enough time to visit the museum. I also bought a couple of tiles, because carrying fragile ceramics around Europe for another two weeks seemed like a good idea.

A lot of what caught my attention inside was ceramic being used as graphic design: advertisements, lettering, and public signs made out of tile.

Plaza de España

The next day I walked from the hotel to NYC Icy and got lotus and chocolate ice cream, then kept going to Plaza de España. It is a pretty sweet building and plaza. The whole place is full of ceramic and stone details that are easy to miss while looking at the scale of it.

The stonework was just as good. Someone cut a bow-tie-shaped joint directly into this railing, and I probably spent longer looking at it than any normal person would.

The downside was that all the carriage rides made the plaza smell like horse shit, especially with the temperature in the high 30s C.

That makes one week away from home. I have made it to Seville, figured out the transit, found the coffee, and bought breakable souvenirs far too early in the trip. The meetup is next.

Gracias por leer.

item.title: Goodbye to the Hard Parts That Never Mattered
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I read Dave Kiss's eulogy for the software engineer and kept coming back to one question.

What exactly are we saying goodbye to?

Shitty regex? Writing another one-off parser for terrible data? Memorizing some weird syntax for no obvious reason? Losing an afternoon to the particular incantation a build system expects before it will do the thing you already understand?

If that is what died, I am not sure it needs a funeral.

Dave's argument is more hopeful than the title suggests. By the end, he opens the casket back up. The skills are still ours. The engineer is still responsible for what ships. Maybe, he writes, we put the wrong name on the headstone.

I agree with most of that. I just do not think we need the headstone at all.

This does not feel like the death of the software engineer to me. It feels like a rebirth.

The toll was never the destination

Software engineering has always contained a lot of work that is only loosely related to the problem being solved.

You need to move a small pile of ugly data from one system to another, so you spend half a day learning the edge cases of a CSV parser. You know exactly what a service should do, but first you have to remember the syntax for a framework you have not touched in six months. You understand the bug, but the fix is buried behind an unfamiliar repository layout, three layers of indirection, and a test command nobody wrote down.

We got good at this work because we had to. Some of it was even fun. There is a real satisfaction in finally landing the regex or finding the one line that made the whole system behave strangely.

But difficulty is not the same thing as value.

Most of this was a toll we paid between understanding a problem and changing the system. It was never the destination. If an agent can take care of more of that translation, I have not become less of an engineer. I have more time for the part that required an engineer in the first place.

The work moved

I use coding agents every day. They can move through a codebase faster than I can, generate a parser in seconds, and usually remember the library call I would have looked up anyway.

They also make bad assumptions, misunderstand local conventions, confidently use an API that does not exist, and declare victory before testing the thing they changed.

The typing got easier. The engineering did not disappear.

I still have to understand the system well enough to know where to look. I have to recognize when a plausible answer is wrong. I have to decide whether a change belongs in the application, a plugin, an operations repository, or nowhere at all. I have to reproduce the failure, choose the tradeoff, test the result, and stand behind what reaches production.

An agent can write the parser. Someone still has to explain the terrible data, notice when a row silently disappears, and decide what should happen when reality violates the format.

That is software engineering.

This is the same shift I wrote about in I Don't Type Every Word You Read. The work did not vanish. It moved. Less of it lives in producing every character by hand. More of it lives in direction, judgment, verification, and responsibility.

I am learning more, not less

One fear I understand is that removing the hard way also removes the learning. If the machine writes the code, how does anyone develop the instincts needed to know whether it is right?

That risk is real. You can accept whatever appears in the diff, run nothing, learn nothing, and ship garbage at a speed that used to be impossible.

You can also use the same tools to walk into parts of computing that were previously too expensive to explore.

I have used agents to rewrite a TypeScript program in Rust, trace production infrastructure across repositories, understand unfamiliar database behavior, build terminal tools, and test ideas that would never have justified a free weekend. I did not emerge from those projects knowing less Rust, less Linux, or less about the systems involved. The agent handled enough of the syntax and scaffolding that I could keep pulling on the interesting thread.

The learning loop got tighter. Ask a question. Inspect the answer. Run the code. Break it. Read the implementation. Correct the assumption. Try again.

That is not a replacement for understanding. It is an extremely fast way to find the edge of your understanding.

The burden is on us to keep crossing that edge. If we use agents only to avoid knowing things, we will become worse engineers. If we use them to reach the next question faster, we can become much better ones.

The canvas got bigger

The part I find most exciting is not that the same ticket takes fewer hours. It is that entirely different projects now fit inside a human life.

Software has always had an unusually high cost between an idea and its first working form. Even a small idea could demand a new language, a framework, an authentication system, deployment, tests, and a pile of glue before you got to find out whether the idea was any good.

That cost killed a lot of ideas before they became code.

Now I can follow more of the strange little "what if" thoughts that make programming fun. What if forum software were a game engine? What if a terminal audiobook player worked exactly like my music player? What if I rebuilt a tool in another language just to understand how it worked?

These are not hypothetical examples. I built them. They taught me about real-time state, media containers, terminal interfaces, systems programming, and the boundaries of the tools helping me.

I do not see a shrinking profession in that. I see a creative medium becoming available at a scale it has never had before.

There are still reasons to worry

None of this means every consequence will be good.

Companies will use the productivity story as cover to cut people. Generated code will create failures at a scale we are not prepared for. The traditional path from junior engineer to experienced engineer is going to change, and I do not think anyone honestly knows what replaces it yet. Access also matters. A profession cannot call itself newly open if the best tools require hundreds of dollars every month.

Those are serious problems. They deserve more than a slogan about AI being a tool or a prediction that everyone will become ten times more productive.

But they are questions about who benefits from the technology, how we teach, and how we organize the work. They are not evidence that software engineering has ceased to exist.

If anything, faster generation makes engineering discipline more important. When producing code was slow, bad decisions accumulated slowly too. Now a bad assumption can become three thousand lines before lunch. Clear requirements, tests, review, observability, and taste do not matter less in that world. They are the only things keeping the increased output useful.

No funeral

I understand the grief in Dave's piece. A way of working that many of us built our identities around is changing very quickly. There are parts of it I will miss too. Solving something the hard way can feel incredible, especially when the hard way was how you learned that you were capable of solving it at all.

But I do not want to confuse the obstacles with the craft.

The craft was never remembering every method signature. It was never manually typing every line or personally wrestling every malformed document into submission. Those were the mechanics available to us at the time.

The craft is understanding a problem deeply enough to change it. It is making tradeoffs with incomplete information. It is noticing the wrong note in a system that technically works. It is taking responsibility for the result.

We still need all of that. Now we get to apply it to more problems, in more domains, with a much larger set of tools.

So I am not ready to bury the software engineer.

We are learning a new way to work. We are building a new layer of technology while learning how to use it, govern it, and teach it. We are shedding some accidental complexity and discovering new kinds underneath. We can attempt things that were impractical a year ago, and we are only beginning to understand what that means.

This is not a eulogy.

The software engineer is just getting started.

item.title: Agent assisted Changelog - 37/52
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
In the last summary, the first paid Agents of Empires tournament was still next. There are now cups, champions, a domain, replays, and enough conversations about tournament formats that I briefly considered duplicating the entrants just to fill a bracket. The software is getting better. My ability to leave the scope alone remains unproven.

The battleground became a cup circuit

Agents of Empires is now live at agents-of-empires.dev. The homepage explains the idea and points to cups; each cup has its own description and tournament history; each tournament has a bracket and links to the actual attempts. The replay defaults to 5x, because watching someone else's infrastructure wait to boot should at least be faster than watching your own.

The usual format is six entrants, two three-agent opening heats, and a final with the two winners plus a wildcard. Publishing a draw and running it are separate operations. That means I can announce the field before spending anything, then run exactly that bracket later.

The first clean OpenCode Cup had DeepSeek win its opening build race in 43.2 seconds and the durable job queue final in 89.8. All three heats finished on their first attempt. No forfeits, no replays. Getting there was less tidy.

Earlier tests produced enough failures that I could not tell whether I was watching poor play or a broken adapter. The fixes included explicit guest model definitions instead of hoping OpenCode refreshed its catalog, making the configured memory floor reach the actual VMs, and keeping the rollout continuity monitor alive for the match's configured duration.

There was also a tournament that crowned a contender after everybody failed. That is a perfectly reasonable way to invent a sport I did not mean to invent. Heat winners now need a durable deployment. Sporting draws and unavailable seats have separate, bounded replay budgets, and an exhausted bracket can end without a champion. Tied wildcard ranks use a seeded lottery, not alphabetical order or the cheapest bill.

Kimi took the first published Vercel Cup. Different routes, different fields, different stories. Still not a model ranking. Replaybook is where I do the evaluation work; this is where I want to pick a contender and watch a race.

One pool, frozen draws

Adding cups made the model lists annoying almost immediately. OpenRouter, OpenCode Go, and Vercel AI Gateway each expose a different slice of the world, and maintaining those lists independently was an invitation to drift.

AoE now has one shared model registry. Each cup selects its provider slice, and season draw --entrants 6 samples a field without requiring the whole eligible pool to enter. The selected entrants and eligible pool are frozen into the draw. Refreshing a catalog tomorrow must not change the tournament I announced today.

The refresh script defaults to a dry run. New discoveries stay disabled until reviewed, and refreshes preserve deliberate access blocks and premium-model opt-ins. Finding a model in a catalog is not proof that my account can run it, or that I want to pay for it.

I also floated a budget cup that draws from whatever is on sale. That remains an idea, not another thing quietly running up a bill in the background.

Same model, different harnesses

The new adapter is for term-llm. The first Harness Cup put it against Claux and OpenCode, all configured for OpenRouter GPT-5.6 Luna, high reasoning, one vCPU, and 768 MiB of memory per guest.

term-llm won in 45.216 seconds. The outside referee verified the service, record round-trip, service restart, and host reboot. OpenCode was outraced. Claux's guest rebooted and the SSH connection dropped, but the retained evidence does not establish who initiated that reboot. There was no referee reboot marker for its seat and no recorded reboot command in its tool trace. That stays an unresolved harness error, not a story about a model deciding to restart its machine.

The accounting needed attention too. Missing provider costs had looked like zero dollars, and token totals did not consistently include cache categories. Future adapter output now normalizes fresh input, cache reads, and cache writes; reporting distinguishes a known total from an incomplete subtotal. The original event logs remain unchanged. Usage captured while losing agents drain after the finish is also not a synchronized race-only measurement.

We recorded this as an exhibition, then published it as a single-round cup. Three entrants and one final are enough. I considered two opening heats with duplicate entries from each harness, then decided to wait for more distinct harnesses. A bracket should describe the competition, not manufacture a need for more seats.

Timecapsule starts with an inbox

The other thread was an archive of Angine de Poitrine material. I wanted to find scattered recordings and links without turning every discovery into a published claim about a performance, its date, or its rights.

Timecapsule is a local prototype for that flow. Internet Archive discovery produces private metadata snapshots in an inbox. I review a candidate, approve it into a Markdown record with source and rights notes, then build a static archive. Repeating discovery does not reset review decisions. An upload date does not silently become a concert date. Approval does not deploy a website or download the recording.

The optional TypeSafe/Jev integration sits between discovery and review. It can suggest relevance and material type from metadata, and I can preview the exact request before making a paid call. It does not watch the video, approve the entry, or decide that I have permission to republish it. I have not run a paid enrichment call yet.

The first implementation has sixteen tests covering the unglamorous parts: deduplication, retained decisions, approval recovery, validation, escaping, private/public separation, and byte-identical offline builds. YouTube discovery and a visual review inbox are not wired in yet. There is no public repository link for this one yet either; it is still local work.

The through-line

This week kept coming back to what a result actually authorizes me to say.

A model being listed does not mean an account can use it. A null charge does not mean the race was free. An SSH disconnect does not identify who rebooted the machine. Finding a recording does not establish its date or give me permission to copy it.

The useful work is in keeping those distinctions visible without making the whole thing miserable to use. I still want the bracket to be fun and the archive to be inviting. I just want the next person clicking through to find the evidence, not a more confident version of my guess.

item.title: Agent assisted Changelog - 36/52
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
One actual week this time. It started with three architecture reviews and ended with a tournament bracket, which is roughly the arc of every project I touch: first find out what is actually broken, then build the thing that was the point all along.

Three reviews, thirty-one issues

I had an agent do a deep review of Claux, Replaybook, and llm-mux as harnesses: runtime, provider boundaries, sandboxing, persistence, observability, and the contracts between them. Each review fanned out to sub-reviewers per subsystem, then every high-severity claim got re-verified against the source before it was allowed into the report. That last step mattered. One reviewer cited line numbers for a file that was a third the length it claimed; the finding was right, the citations were not.

The Claux review became twenty-five GitHub issues with file and line references, a failure scenario, and a suggested fix each. The two that stung were the boring ones: OpenAI's context-overflow body puts the useful identifier in code while the classifier read type first, so auto-compaction on overflow had never fired for a first-party provider; and the Anthropic stream reader never looked at stop_reason, so a truncated answer was reported to Replaybook as a completed one. Both are still open, on purpose, because the fix that unblocks them landed first.

The llm-mux review found a dangling-symlink escape in the apply path and a project-config trust filter that stripped command but not env. Both got fixed the same week, along with side-effect-free dry runs and bounded retries, and shipped as v20260905.0.0. The Replaybook review found that the benchmark classifier had been reading a script that was missing from every execution snapshot, one real provider key in twenty-three retained transcripts from before the credential proxy existed, and a publisher that validated only the current release. The key got rotated. The rest is on the list.

Claux learned to say why it failed

Claux went through six releases this week, from v20260904.0.0 to v20260909.0.0, and closed thirteen issues. The one I care about is the failure taxonomy.

Until now ApiFailureKind had four variants and no transient class. A 429, a 503, a connection reset, and an expired credential all fell into Other, ended the turn, and left the process with exit status 1 and a sentence on stderr. Replaybook classified those sentences with a regex table. Agents of Empires could only tell "the model failed" from "the SSH session died" by checking for status 255 and a reboot marker.

Now failures are typed: rate_limited, unavailable, network, authentication, model_not_found, policy_rejection, protocol_error, cancelled, and the three recovery kinds that already existed. Transient kinds are retried up to three times with backoff and jitter, honoring a capped Retry-After, gated on the existing rule that a partially surfaced tool batch is never reissued, and the backoff sleep is selected against the cancellation token so Ctrl-C during a thirty-second wait returns immediately. One-shot JSON is written on failure too, with a null result and an outcome.failure object, and the exit code encodes the kind: 10 through 18, chosen to never collide with SSH's 255 or the shell's 126 to 128-plus-signal range. That last constraint exists because the Agents of Empires adapter runs Claux over SSH and had been attributing transport drops to the player.

The rest of the week's Claux work was the kind of thing that only shows up after a review: permission rules with globs (Bash(git *), Edit(src/**)) and a pre-tool hook that can answer allow, deny, or ask as JSON; a child-process environment built from the configuration's own api_key_env names instead of a fixed pattern list; bounded Bash output capture that drains without storing; unique tool_use ids even when a gateway repeats them; a compaction marker that no longer produces two consecutive user messages; a bounded api_key_cmd with a Windows shell; NAT64 and 6to4 ranges in the WebFetch policy; and a SHA256SUMS asset on every release so the two consumers can stop computing digests locally. Separately I shipped background Bash jobs owned by the session, a live tool-activity line in the TUI, terminal-mode restoration on every shutdown path, and task-preserving compaction. The unit test count went from 473 to 524 over the week.

Agents of Empires stopped blaming the controller

The most useful number from the Agents of Empires review was not in the code. (Background on the arena is in Not a Leaderboard, a Battleground and The Battleground Has a Map Now.) In the two four-arena suite runs on disk, 29 of 72 agent appearances were recorded as controller failures with the reason "post-match drain deadline expired." Eleven of GLM 5.3's twelve appearances were in that bucket. None of those agents had been failed by the controller. They had lost the race: a rival reached durable first, the match froze, and anyone still building was terminated at the drain deadline and counted as infrastructure. The leaderboard was honest about the label and wrong about the meaning.

That is now an AgentOutraced event, an incomplete terminal state, and a player outcome ranked by the milestones the agent had verified, which is what the spec always said should happen. AgentTerminated still exists for genuine controller kills, so old event logs reduce unchanged. Re-rendering the August 20 run under the new accounting turns GLM 5.3 from "eleven controller failures" into "zero durable, eleven outraced, six of sixty milestones," which is the true and considerably less flattering result. The evaluated rate on the site goes from under half to over ninety percent without touching a verifier. The adapter also now reads Claux's typed failures and exit codes, so a rate limit is unavailable and a context overflow is failed, and a present result file no longer implies success. Both consumers pin claux v20260908.0.0 by SHA-256 now, and I talked myself out of a "latest" default: the pin is part of the evidence.

Then I wanted a weekly season with a bracket and random draws, and the draw-first idea turned out to be the interesting part. A season manifest names a fleet of any size and an arena pool. season draw derives heat composition, the arena per round, and every seat from a published seed (season id, week, optional salt) and writes draw.json before any inference runs, so anyone can re-derive the bracket. Heats are three seats because arenas declare three territories; byes and milestone-ranked wildcards fill the rounds for fleets that do not divide evenly. A second, secret variation seed goes to verifiers as AOE_SCENARIO_SEED; only its SHA-256 commitment is published with the draw, and week.json reveals it after the week completes, so competitors cannot predict verifier-side values and anyone can check the reveal. A seat whose result is unavailable earns the heat one replay; a repeat forfeits and is never a loss. The race still stops at the first durable deployment. Losing it is the result.

The report got a season page, a bracket page per week with every seat's outcome as durable, outraced, failed, or forfeit, and the homepage became a tournament hub. season run has not driven a real VM yet; the draw has been verified against the real manifests and the accounting against fixtures. The first paid week is next.

Replaybook became an evidence workspace

Replaybook's site stopped being a leaderboard with a compare tab and became an Evidence workspace: dark surfaces, a per-attempt wall where a fully evaluated three-attempt cell is red at 0 or 1, yellow at 2, green at 3, and gray when the evidence is incomplete or unavailable, with the old compare and explore URLs redirecting and preserving their selections. Models are now family cards with provider and reasoning configurations underneath; the previous "41 models" was counting configurations, and the honest numbers are 29 served model IDs and 43 provider, model, and reasoning combinations, kept separate pending verified aliases.

New evidence landed too. Claude Fable 5.1 went 32 of 33 repairs across the combined text and visual run; Gemini 3.8 Flash went 24 of 33 with protocol failures and much higher token use. The large OpenCode Go core run reached 114 of 120 valid results after retries, with the remainder still returning provider-unavailable on the Nix disk-pressure cells. OpenRouter's six-model core baseline is published with Sonnet replacing Ox Alpha. New host matrices require an invocation-level provider, and I backfilled provider metadata on the older OpenRouter results by hand, which is exactly the kind of "never hand edit" activity the repository rules exist to make uncomfortable.

The part where the agent wrote a URL into my history

Two things this week were the agent's doing and my fault for not looking.

First, a deep review of Claux was published as a hosted artifact on claude.ai without my asking. Private to my account, but a security review of my own code and two downstream repos is not something I want leaving the machine by default. I turned the artifact tool off in settings.

Second, and worse: every commit the agent wrote this week ended with a Claude-Session: trailer linking to the conversation. It was an attribution convention the harness told it to follow, formatted like a Co-Authored-By line, and it applied it mechanically to around thirty commits across three repos without a word. I noticed after seventeen of them had gone out in tagged Claux releases. The unpushed ones were rewritten; the pushed ones are inert URLs only my login can open, and I decided a force-push and three moved release tags were not worth it. The setting is off now.

The lesson is not "agents are careless." It is that I had drawn the caution boundary around actions the agent takes and not around text it writes into my artifacts. A commit message is an action. So is a filename. The agent, to its credit, said exactly that when I asked it how it had missed the obvious.

Smaller things

I started looking at what leaving Hyprland would take. Nothing has moved yet, but there is now a river config on a branch in my dotfiles: same keys, gruvbox, no effects, with swaybg, swayidle, swaylock, grim, and slurp standing in for the Hypr-branded pieces. The surprise was that river 0.4 is not a window manager anymore. It is a compositor that does rendering, protocols, Xwayland, and outputs, and expects a separate window manager process speaking a stable protocol, in any language, hot-swappable, crash-survivable. The old tiling river is river-classic. The config targets classic and has not been booted into yet, but the 0.4 split is exactly the substrate for a declarative, Nix-shaped window manager that I have wanted and never had the appetite to write a compositor for.

Agent Zen Garden is submitted, live, and being used by people who are not me. Heart Eyes Tattoo got real artists and a mobile-first pass.

The through-line

This week was about attribution, in both senses.

Replaybook and Agents of Empires both had numbers that were correctly labeled and wrongly understood: "controller failure" for a lost race, "41 models" for 41 configurations. Claux had the same problem one layer down, where a rate limit and a bad credential and a truncated answer all produced the same sentence. Fixing those meant adding a type, an event, or a column, not changing what was measured. The measurements were fine. The names were lying by omission.

And the same week, the tools attributing my work to an agent session did it in a way I had not consented to, because I had not asked. The boundary I want around agents is the one I keep building into the benchmarks: say what you did, say who did it, and make the label mean the same thing to the next person who reads it.

item.title: Agent assisted Changelog - 35/52
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Two weeks since the last changelog. The numbering is still pretending this is one week, but the work did not take the hint. I spent the gap running model matrices, building a WebMCP project, recording a demo, and waiting for enough provider outages to make the word "unavailable" feel like a product feature.

Last time, Replaybook had become a benchmark system and Agent Zen Garden was a promising little experiment. This time both projects had to survive contact with other people: other providers, other browsers, other machines, and a submission form with a hard deadline.

Replaybook stopped pretending every run was the same

Replaybook got a more honest shape.

The benchmark site now separates text and visual inputs, groups models by provider, shows the scenario set and harness behind each result, and keeps comparison boundaries visible. Provider identity is part of an invocation, not something inferred from a model name after the fact. A Luna run through OpenRouter, OpenCode Go, or Vercel is now three distinct pieces of evidence.

That sounds obvious. It took several rounds of pages, publisher assertions, backfilled provenance, and one afternoon of asking why a model page only showed six models when I had run many more.

The scenario catalog grew too. The visual set now includes topology drift, metrics regression, and a deployment timeline. The last one gives the agent a timeline image and asks it to reconcile the observed sequence with a live system. The image is evidence, not an answer key. The repair still has to work, survive service restart, and survive a host reboot.

The planner now knows about providers and can describe coverage gaps without quietly mixing incompatible cohorts. The publisher can compose independently run matrices when their harness, scenario, attempt, and verifier boundaries match. Missing provider attempts can be resumed instead of forcing a complete matrix to start over. Failure inspection became a report rather than a pile of paths in a terminal.

The numbers are finally interesting because the boundaries are explicit. A 36-trial OpenCode visual cohort finished with 34 evaluated repairs. DeepSeek, Kimi, and MiniMax each went 9/9; Qwen finished 7/9. A Vercel cohort across Luna, Sol, and GLM 5.3 Flash went 27/27 after I added credits; the earlier free endpoint mostly taught me what a provider interruption looks like. OpenRouter Luna's 24-trial core run went 22/24. HY4 preview went 8/9. The same visual timeline gave Sonnet 3/3, Opus 1/3 after two timeouts, and Terra 3/3.

None of those is a universal model ranking. They are slices with different providers, prices, and failure surfaces. That is the point. The benchmark can now say which slice it is showing instead of printing one confident table over the top of all of them.

The larger OpenCode run also demonstrated why this matters. A 120-trial command started with the wrong adapter flags, then met a day when several providers were unavailable. I stopped it rather than count empty sessions as failed repairs. A benchmark that records its own orchestration failure is more useful than one that turns every red line into a model verdict.

Claux learned to leave better evidence

Claux spent this stretch becoming less dramatic and more dependable.

Image input crossed the boundary from a prompt description into the agent protocol, which is what made the visual Replaybook scenarios possible. Context limits now come from provider model metadata where available, so compaction no longer depends on a stale hand-maintained number. Tokenizer fingerprinting can resume and emit a Markdown report, which is useful when a model's public name does not tell me whether two endpoints share an actual tokenizer.

Then came the boring failures that are only boring after they are fixed:

  • streamed output is cleared before a provider retry;
  • cancelled Responses streams clear their cursor;
  • compacted history stays available for continuation;
  • child processes cannot inherit credentials accidentally; and
  • TUI resume switches sessions without leaving the old one attached.

Provider API-key login flows, usage status, and adapter setup also became first-class commands. The usage command reports what the authenticated key actually exposes and says "unavailable" when the provider does not expose a remaining balance. It does not invent a monthly subscription price from thin air.

The current release is v20260902.0.1. The crate passed 1,000 downloads while I was busy chasing a retry bug, which is a nice reminder that software can find users while its author is still arguing with a terminal. The release also closed the most severe open issues around cancellation, compaction, retries, credential leakage, and session recovery.

The useful Claux feature this week was not a new model integration. It was the ability to tell the difference between a model making a bad operational choice, a provider refusing a request, and the harness losing its own state. Those three things all look like "the agent failed" if the recording is too small.

Agent Zen Garden went from experiment to submission

I built Agent Zen Garden because I wanted to see what WebMCP felt like when attached to something more useful than a button that says hello. It is now a small design sandbox where an agent can select a layout, inspect its named slots, change copy and styles, add an image, and save the result for a human to judge.

The important loop is:

list_layouts
select_layout
examine_layout
set_style
set_copy
add_font
add_image

The native browser tools are thin. The server owns validation and persistence, and an HTTP fallback keeps the project usable when a browser does not support WebMCP yet. A selected layout gets its own workspace. SQLite stores the design name and optional agent/provider/model metadata, so a share link still works after a restart. A public Designs page makes the results visible to people who are not running an agent.

The project is running at agentzen.garden, with the API behind Caddy on stream. It has persistence, rate limiting, social metadata, an ISC license, and GoatCounter tracking. The first useful event was a design called “Signal After Dark” appearing in the preview and share paths. That was the moment the site stopped being a demo I had to explain and became a place where somebody else could leave evidence.

I wrote I Let an Agent Design a Portfolio Page about the first session, then recorded a short demo with an agent operating the tools in the browser. The video was submitted to the WebMCP Challenge before the extended deadline. It is a small project, but the interaction is a different shape from “generate me a website”: the human supplies direction and taste, while the agent makes precise changes against a constrained, inspectable design surface.

The font-generator experiment taught the companion lesson. Passing an SVG path to a model is not the same thing as letting it see a glyph and infer a style. The first versions produced twenty-six copies of A, then paths in the wrong Bezier format, then an alphabet that technically existed but looked nothing like the input. The failure was not that agents cannot understand an alphabet. It was that the app kept asking a backend function to manufacture an answer instead of actually sending the visual evidence to a vision-capable model.

Agents of Empires got a real build race

Agents of Empires finally has a visual Blueprint Build arena. Three agents receive a service contract and a blank machine, then compete to build a deployment that survives the referee's checks. The map is driven by the same milestone events that decide the match; it is not an animation pasted over a terminal log.

The first version had a humiliating bug: the arena called agents with no vision while asking them to work from a diagram. Once the fleet used vision-capable models, the match became legible. The live terminal now shows the model for each territory, the controller fails fast on harness outages, and adapter process groups are cleaned up instead of continuing after the match ends.

Luna won repeated three-round series by reaching a durable deployment first. Ox and Kimi produced useful attempts, but several rounds never reached the gateway verification milestone. That is not a conclusion about their general ability. It is a reminder that an arena needs to show whether an agent failed the system, the provider, or the starting conditions before anyone starts calling it a strategy game.

Small projects kept becoming systems

gym-jams shipped publicly and got its own post. It turns an album into a workout by letting deterministic audio analysis provide duration, tempo arcs, energy, and pulse stability, then asking a model to map that structure onto one sentence of intent. The model never needed to hear the music. It needed an honest description of what the music was doing.

The app also gave me a nice refusal: when I requested a twenty-minute recovery session from a record containing fourteen and a half minutes of calm, it reported the mismatch instead of padding the plan with imaginary easy sections. That is a small example of the same rule Replaybook keeps teaching me: a plausible answer is not necessarily an accurate one.

I kept working on Heart Eyes Tattoo as a tiny mobile-first studio site. It now has About, Artists, and individual artist pages, with booking routed from each artist rather than pretending the studio shares one calendar. The artist index is intentionally just names over a rotating set of the SVG shapes from my icon collection. A yellow-and-coral frame, flowing stripes, pink burst, and coral starburst cycle through the five artists. The cards are visual indexes, not five copies of the same biography waiting to be filled in.

The Discourse instance on stream also became less theoretical: the directory plugin was rebuilt behind Caddy, Mailgun handled the first successful login mail, and the directory's DNS and service records are now part of the same deployment conversation as the rest of the little sites. Arch Linux remains perfectly capable of hosting Discourse, provided Docker, DNS, SMTP, and the operator all agree on what day it is.

The through-line

The last two weeks were mostly about turning agent output into something another person can inspect.

Replaybook now shows the provider, harness, scenario, and evidence boundary instead of making a leaderboard do all the storytelling. Claux keeps enough state to explain whether a continuation really continued. Agent Zen Garden stores the design that an agent made instead of leaving it in a browser tab. Agents of Empires puts the model and verifier events on the same map. Even gym-jams works because the model gets a measurable description rather than a request to pretend it heard something.

The easy version of all these projects is a clever response in a terminal. The harder version is the one that survives a restart, a provider outage, a second person clicking the link, or a skeptical look at the artifact afterward.

That is where the interesting work keeps ending up: not in making the agent say more, but in making the boundary around what it did harder to misunderstand.

item.title: I Let an Agent Design a Portfolio Page
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I built a little website and then handed the website to an agent.

Not the whole website. The agent did not get a blank repository and a vague instruction to "make it nice." It got a page with a few fixed layouts and a set of tools for changing the parts I had decided were safe to change.

The project is Agent Zen Garden, and it is now running at agentzen.garden.

I wanted to see what WebMCP felt like when it was attached to something more interesting than a button that says hello. The answer, after a weekend of wiring and one very productive Codex session, is a small design sandbox where an agent can build a page and a human can decide whether it is any good.

The blank canvas problem

Agents are very good at making changes. They are less reliable at deciding which changes are worth making when the possible surface area is infinite.

Give an agent an empty directory and "design a portfolio" and it can produce anything from a lovely landing page to six hundred lines of gradients and a navigation system that only works in its own imagination. The problem is not that it cannot write CSS. The problem is that "good" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

So the garden starts with constraints. There are a few HTML layouts with named slots: a headline, a navigation area, an image, a set of cards, a footer. The structure is fixed. The agent can inspect the available slots and selectors, then change the copy, typography, colors, spacing, and images without having to invent an entire application architecture first.

The constraints are not meant to make the agent less creative. They make the creative decisions visible.

The tool loop

The page exposes a small design API through WebMCP. An agent can discover the tools directly from the page when the browser supports the native API, and the same operations remain available as ordinary HTTP endpoints for everything else.

The basic loop is:

list_layouts
select_layout name="A Quiet Portfolio"
examine_layout
set_style
set_copy
add_font
add_image
export_pdf

examine_layout is the important one. It returns the named slots, the CSS selectors, and the current stylesheet. The agent gets a map before it starts moving furniture around.

set_style merges declarations into a selector's existing rule. set_copy updates a named slot rather than asking the agent to rewrite arbitrary HTML. add_font loads a Google Font, and add_image puts a public image URL into an image or background slot. At the end, export_pdf renders the result with Chromium so the output is not just whatever happened to look right in the agent's text response.

The native WebMCP layer is deliberately thin. It reads the page's manifest and registers each operation with document.modelContext. The server still owns the implementation. A browser agent gets page-specific tools; the server gets to keep its validation, filesystem writes, and live reload in one place.

I gave it a portfolio

For the first real session, I gave Codex the portfolio layout and let it work through the tool loop. It inspected the structure, chose a direction, changed the type and spacing, replaced the placeholder copy, and iterated against the actual page instead of describing a page it hoped existed.

The useful part was not that it could call set_style. Any competent agent can write:

.hero-headline {
  letter-spacing: -0.04em;
  font-size: clamp(3rem, 9vw, 8rem);
}

The useful part was that the change happened in a running design surface with known selectors, and the next inspection reflected what was actually there. It could make a change, look at the result, and make a smaller change. That is closer to working with a designer's file than to asking a chatbot for a block of CSS and pasting it in with your fingers crossed.

I still had opinions. I still said when something was too busy, when the spacing felt wrong, and when a clever treatment was not helping. The agent was fast at the exhaustive part: trying the variations, keeping the selectors straight, and applying the boring changes consistently. I supplied the direction and the vetoes.

That division feels more honest than pretending the agent has taste in the same way a person does.

A design should survive the process

The first version stored sessions in memory. That was fine until I asked the obvious question: what happens when I send somebody a link and then restart the service?

The answer was a 404, because the files were on disk but the server had forgotten that the session existed. The filesystem had a better memory than the application.

Now selecting a layout creates an isolated workspace:

workspaces/<session-id>/
├── index.html
└── style.css

The session catalog lives in SQLite. It stores the layout, creation time, and optional metadata such as the design name, agent, provider, model, and harness. The files and the catalog come back when the process restarts.

select_layout returns both a live preview URL and a share URL. Recent designs are available from the design catalog, and agents can use list_designs or GET /api/designs to discover them. The catalog is intentionally simple. It is a list of experiments, not a social network that needs a feed algorithm.

There is no account system or permissions model yet. A share link is an unguessable UUID, not an access-control policy. This is a design sandbox, not the place I would put somebody's banking dashboard.

What WebMCP changes

I could build most of this with a local agent and a command-line API. The interesting difference is that the tools belong to the page.

The agent does not need a separate integration that knows the garden's private endpoints. It visits the page, discovers the manifest, and gets operations that are specific to the surface in front of it. A different page could expose different tools: a music sequencer could provide tracks and effects, a diagram editor could provide nodes and edges, and a data dashboard could provide filters and annotations.

That makes a website feel less like a document an agent is looking at and more like an application an agent can participate in.

It is also not magic. WebMCP support is still browser-dependent, and the fallback path matters. The HTTP API means a non-WebMCP client can still create and edit a session. The browser integration is an additional affordance, not a requirement that every user install a particular agent in a particular browser.

The line between useful and ridiculous

There is a version of this project that is just a website builder with an agent bolted onto it. That is not especially interesting. We have had website builders for a long time, and most of them have fewer opinions about CSS than I do.

The bit I want to keep exploring is the boundary between human intent and agent execution:

  • the human picks the direction and says what feels wrong;
  • the agent traces the available structure and makes precise changes;
  • the page shows the result instead of returning a paragraph about the result;
  • both of us can keep iterating without losing the state of the work.

That is a small thing, but it is a different shape of interaction from "generate me a website." It is closer to handing an assistant a design file and saying, "make the headline feel less timid, but leave the rest alone."

What's next

I want to add more layouts, better visual inspection, and a way to compare versions of a design without turning the garden into a full Git client. A comment or annotation layer would be useful too: point at a section, leave a note, let the agent make a change, then decide whether the result is closer.

The danger is obvious. Every time I add another tool, I make the sandbox more capable and the idea less clear. The garden should stay small enough that a person can understand what the agent is allowed to do.

For now, it is a page with a few layouts, a persistent workspace, and an agent that can actually change what is on screen.

I made a tool to let an agent design a website. It immediately made me want to design a better website for the tool.

That seems about right.

Source: github.com/ducks/agent-zen-garden

item.title: gym-jams: Turn an Album Into a Workout
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I had what I thought was a prerequisite question: are models any good at sound recognition? I wanted an app that takes an album and generates a workout plan mapped onto it, and I assumed the hard part was teaching a model to hear music.

Wrong question. The app never needed model hearing at all.

The Idea

An album has a fixed length, a track order, a tempo map, and an energy arc. That's a workout plan wearing headphones. The design rule that makes gym-jams work is simple: the album is the timer. The session starts with track 1 and ends when the record does. No mid-session decisions, no phone fiddling between sets. When the record stops, you're done.

gym-jams init
